summary: Full-extraction pass over 20 international documents: FATF grey lists, the FATF/OECD 2023 report, the FinCEN St Kitts advisory and its rescission, the UK 2023 visa memorandum, the IMF ECCU 2024 Article IV and WP/15/93, six versions of the OECD CRS high-risk list, the OECS CBI memorandum and two releases, US Proclamation 10998 and the 2000 INCSR. Most are policy texts already reflected in events; new rows are the OECS US$200,000 minimum per programme, Dominica and Grenada economic-citizenship figures from 2000, ECCU fiscal balances excluding CBI, St Kitts fiscal statistics net of ECP from WP/15/93, and fraud and high-risk figures from the FATF/OECD case studies.

observations.location: Dominica country section, para 3
observations.quote: Between 1996 and 2000, the GOD issued approximately 500 economic citizenships.
observations.notes: Rounded ('approximately'). Counts 'economic citizenships'; whether family members are included is not stated. US State Department relaying Dominica government information.

observations.location: Dominica country section, para 3
observations.quote: The GOD indicated that in the first quarter of 2000 it had earned approximately US $1.9 million from sales of passports.
observations.notes: Government of Dominica figure relayed by the US State Department; rounded ('approximately'). 'Earned from sales of passports': whether fees only or all receipts is not stated.

observations.location: Grenada country section, para 3
observations.quote: Grenada has issued approximately 300 economic citizenships, and claims that proper background checks are made.
observations.notes: Rounded ('approximately'). Period not stated: presumably since the 1997 Act; dataset convention 'to' the report's month (issued 1 March 2001). Whether family members are included is not stated.

events.title: New Prime Minister suspends Dominica passport sales
events.description: On taking office in January 2000, Prime Minister Roosevelt Douglas suspended sales of economic citizenship; he reversed the decision in April 2000.
events.quote: Upon taking office in January 2000, Prime Minister (PM) Roosevelt Douglas suspended passport sales, but in April 2000, reversed his decision.

events.title: Dominica resumes passport sales
events.description: The suspension of January 2000 was reversed in April 2000.
events.quote: but in April 2000, reversed his decision.

events.title: Dominica says it has suspended economic citizenship under international pressure
events.description: The government claimed to have suspended the programme after Canada threatened visa requirements for Dominican passport holders; the report also mentions a case of 11 Chinese nationals who tried to enter Canada on Dominican passports.
events.quote: In August 2000, the GOD claimed to have suspended the program in the face of international pressure-in particular, the Government of Canada threatened to impose visa requirements on Dominican passport holders.

events.title: Grenada takes over offshore bank whose founder had bought a Grenadian passport
events.description: The government took control of the First International Bank of Grenada in August 2000; the US report says its founder had changed his name and purchased a Grenadian passport. The bank reportedly owed about 6,000 depositors nearly US$150 million.
events.location: Grenada country section, paras on FIBG
events.quote: changed his name, and purchased a Grenadian passport

events.title: St Vincent and the Grenadines creates a legal framework for economic citizenship
events.description: The US report (covering 2000) says SVG had recently created the legislative framework for an economic citizenship programme and projected about US$4.5 million from passport sales in 2000.
events.location: St. Vincent and the Grenadines country section, para 3
events.quote: Recently, SVG created the legislative framework for an economic citizenship program

new_indicators.name: Subsidised credit backed by a CBI-financed development fund, percent of GDP
new_indicators.definition: Credit facilities that banks extend at below-market rates against zero- or low-interest deposits placed by a national development fund financed by citizenship- or residence-by-investment money (e.g. St Kitts SIDF), as a stock at a date (breakdown category=facilities_outstanding), or the annual interest subsidy they imply (category=annual_subsidy), in percent of GDP, as stated by the source.
new_indicators.notes: Proposed by extract-cbi-intl3 for IMF WP/15/93 Box 5 (SIDF facilities 'about 1.5 percent of GDP by end-2013', subsidies 'about 0.05 percent of GDP per year'). No existing indicator covers NDF-backed lending.

ledger.contains: US State Department INCSR 2000 (issued 1 March 2001), Money Laundering and Financial Crimes volume: introduction on offshore centres (lists Belize, Dominica, Grenada, St Kitts/Nevis, St Vincent and Nauru as selling 'economic citizenship'), definitions for the separate Offshore Financial Services Chart (a linked page, not part of this stored file), US SAR statistics, and country reports on money laundering for about 200 jurisdictions. Programme content: Dominica (US$50,000 payment or US$75,000 bonds; about 500 economic citizenships 1996-2000; about US$1.9 million from passport sales in Q1 2000; suspension Jan 2000, reversal Apr 2000, claimed suspension Aug 2000); Grenada (1997 Act, about US$40,000 for a family of five, about 300 economic citizenships, FIBG founder bought a Grenadian passport); St Kitts and Nevis (programme under the Citizenship Act of 1984, already in the data); St Vincent (new legal framework, US$4.5 million projection, already recorded); Tonga sells economic citizenship (already recorded). Everything else (offshore banks, IBCs, gaming licences, SAR counts, AML laws, FIBG deposits) is not about the programmes. Rows already taken from this source (VCT projection, two events) were not repeated.

IMF Working Paper WP/15/93 (May 2015, 34 pages) on economic citizenship programmes. Same file (same checksum) as kna-imf-wp-15-93 and dma-imf-wp-15-93, both already reviewed; this pass took only what those passes left and filed it here. Added now: Portugal golden-visa inflows up to 13% of 2014 gross FDI; EB-5 visas 2% of annual US immigration; St Kitts budget support about 5½% of GDP; Box 2 statistics of St Kitts' fiscal balance net of ECP 1979-2013 (mean, standard deviation, maximum, minimum, and of its cyclical component) and the average and cumulative deficits of the three shock episodes printed on the Box 2 chart; SIDF subsidised credit facilities about 1.5% of GDP at end-2013 and their 0.05%-of-GDP annual subsidy; Table 1 rows for France (EUR 10 million) and Switzerland (CHF 250,000/year). Already in the data from the sister ids: Table 1 and Table 3 terms, Box 1 fee and SIDF figures, Box 5 SIDF tables, Malta, Portugal, US EB-5 and Austria figures, Table 2 suspensions (closure events exist from other sources). Not recorded on purpose: words not numbers (EB-5 visas 'five-fold' 2010-2013; 'about half' of UK economic visas to Chinese and Russians); rounded restatements of table values in the text; consolidated central-government aggregates (not programme figures); sovereign wealth fund tables for non-CBI funds (Tuvalu, Palau, Kiribati, Timor-Leste, PNG; Tonga's passport-funded trust fund has no amounts); charts without printed values (Figures 1-6, Box 1 charts, Figure 2a approvals by nationality).

ledger.contains: IMF Country Report 24/93 (April 2024, 85 pages): ECCU 2024 Article IV staff report on common policies, with press release, selected indicators, staff appraisal, tables 1-8 (region and country macro, fiscal, debt, BOP, banking), annexes (past advice, risk matrix, external assessment, Anguilla and Montserrat, social assistance, fuel prices, credit unions) and statistical issues. Programme content: ECCU-wide central government overall balance excluding CBI revenue 2019-2025 (Table 1 and the identical selected-indicators table), the text's rounded underlying deficits for 2021 and 2023 and the projection of about 3 percent of GDP by 2028; qualitative statements on dependence on CBI inflows, CBI-linked bank deposits and construction, CBI-related FDI not separately recorded, the five CBI countries, and the recommendation of common CBI standards and minimum pricing (event already recorded). No country-level CBI revenue or application numbers are printed; country fiscal tables (Table 3) have no CBI lines. Charts have no printed CBI values. All other content is general macroeconomics, out of scope.

Joint FATF/OECD report 'Misuse of Citizenship and Residency by Investment Programmes' (November 2023, 62 pages): ecosystem overview, threats and vulnerabilities, case studies (Portugal, Cyprus, Greece, St Kitts and Nevis, UK, US, Bangladesh, Antigua and Barbuda, Malta, China, Türkiye, Ireland, New Zealand), corruption and tax risks, mitigation measures. Programme numbers: EPRS EU totals 2011-2019 (already recorded); three politically linked persons granted Maltese citizenship in 2016; US investor-fraud cases (nearly USD 21 million misappropriated, case from 2001; more than USD 50 million collected by an EB-5 scheme, 2017 plea); UK sham-investment fees (GBP 200,000 and GBP 400,000 per applicant); Greek EUR 250,000 residence threshold. Not recorded on purpose: Dominica CBI passport sales 'one third' of GDP in 2016 and CBI revenue 'nearly a third' of GDP in some countries (words, not printed numbers); case details that are not programme figures (properties bought under EUR 100,000 in a Greek case, a RMB 2.75 million transfer in a Chinese case, simulated GBP 1 million and 2 million investments, homes worth nearly USD 1 million); programme launch years (1984, 1986, 1990) and the Irish IIP closure in February 2023, already in the data from other sources. No tables or charts with values.

Signed memorandum of agreement (7 scanned pages, OCR) between the OECS states with CBI programmes (Antigua and Barbuda, Dominica, Grenada, St Kitts and Nevis, Saint Lucia): purpose; pricing (US$200,000 harmonised minimum by 30 June 2024, net of commissions, changes only by unanimity); information sharing via a JRCC portal; transparency to parliaments and audits; a regional regulator by 30 June 2024; security screening; agent and marketing standards (no 'visa-free access' marketing); training; dispute resolution; non-binding legal effect; signature blocks. Added: the US$200,000 minimum as a rule for each of the five programmes. Signing events already recorded. Same file (same checksum) as dma-oecs-cbi-moa-2024, which is not in this batch: its content is covered by these rows and needs no separate extraction.

OECS media release (22 June 2024) on implementing the CBI memorandum of agreement: the five signatories, the US$200,000 minimum price for any CBI option from 1 July 2024, discounting declared illegal, a planned 7-member Interim Regulatory Commission (one member from each of the five countries, the OECS Commission and the ECCB) and its functions; links the signed memorandum. Added: the US$200,000 minimum for each of the five programmes (the effective-date event was already recorded). The commission's size is in the existing event description; no other numbers.

St Kitts and Nevis Information Service release (22 March 2024) on the memorandum of agreement signed by Antigua and Barbuda, Dominica, Grenada and St Kitts and Nevis (dated 20 March 2024): US$200,000 harmonised minimum by 30 June 2024 net of commissions, transparency, regional authority, agent and marketing standards, training; St Kitts programme since 1984, regulation changes in December 2022 and July 2023, minimum raised to US$250,000 by July 2023. Added: the US$200,000 minimum for the four signatories and the St Kitts US$250,000 minimum. Signing, the 2023 changes and the 2023 US-Caribbean principles are already events from other sources. The rest of the page is unrelated news headlines.

FATF 'Jurisdictions under Increased Monitoring' statement after the 2-4 March 2022 plenary: the grey list with progress notes for Albania, Barbados, Burkina Faso, Cambodia, Cayman Islands, Haiti, Jamaica, Jordan, Mali, Malta, Morocco, Myanmar, Nicaragua, Pakistan, Panama, Philippines, Senegal, South Sudan, Syria, Turkey, Uganda, UAE, Yemen, Zimbabwe. It does not mention investment migration programmes and has no programme numbers. The UAE listing is already an event; several other listed jurisdictions run programmes (Malta, Turkey, Cambodia, Jordan, Panama, Barbados, Cayman Islands, Philippines) but no event was added because the document does not link the listing to them.

FATF 'Jurisdictions under Increased Monitoring' statement of 23 February 2024: grey list (Bulgaria, Burkina Faso, Cameroon, DR Congo, Croatia, Haiti, Jamaica, Kenya, Mali, Mozambique, Namibia, Nigeria, Philippines, Senegal, South Africa, South Sudan, Syria, Tanzania, Türkiye, Vietnam, Yemen) and jurisdictions removed (Barbados, Gibraltar, Uganda, UAE). No mention of investment migration programmes and no programme numbers. The UAE removal is already an event; no events added for other programme jurisdictions because the document does not link the listing to them.

FinCEN advisory FIN-2014-A004 (20 May 2014, 2 pages, stamped rescinded). Same file (same checksum) as kna-fincen-advisory-2014, which was reviewed complete: its terms (US$400,000 real estate, US$250,000 SIDF contribution) and events (advisory, 2013 suspension of Iranian nationals) are already recorded there. Nothing left to extract.

FinCEN web page for advisory FIN-2014-A004, marked rescinded as of 24 February 2026, with the full 2014 advisory text (St Kitts CBI terms of US$400,000 real estate or US$250,000 SIDF contribution, Iranian nationals, due-diligence guidance, SAR keyword 'SKN Passport'). The rescission event is recorded; the 2014 terms are the same text already recorded under kna-fincen-advisory-2014 and were not repeated.

St Kitts and Nevis Citizenship Unit release (27 February 2026) confirming FinCEN's rescission of the 2014 advisory on 24 February 2026; lists reforms (statutory body with a board, biometrics, interviews, audits) and says a mandatory genuine-link requirement will be introduced in 2026. No numbers. The rescission is an event; the genuine-link plan is already an event from the CIU chairman's December 2025 update.

UK Home Office explanatory memorandum to HC 1715 (19 July 2023): visa regime for Dominica, Honduras, Namibia, Timor-Leste and Vanuatu from 15:00 on 19 July 2023, citing abuse of Dominica's and Vanuatu's CBI schemes; four-week transition; transit visas; Honduras treaty suspension. Both CBI visa events are recorded. Only other number is the visit-visa service standard (about 15 working days), not a programme figure.

US Proclamation 10998 (16 Dec 2025, 90 FR 59717): full or partial entry restrictions on nationals of many countries; justifications cite CBI without residency as a vetting risk. Antigua and Barbuda and Dominica are partially restricted because they have 'historically had CBI without residency' (both events recorded). Other country sections cite visa-overstay rates (not programme figures); Tonga is restricted for overstays, not for its former passport sales. No programme numbers.

OECD CRS web page 'Residence/Citizenship by investment schemes', version last updated 22 October 2018: list of 30 potentially high-risk CBI/RBI schemes in 21 jurisdictions, criteria (personal income tax rate under 10% on offshore financial assets and no physical presence of at least 90 days) and FAQ for financial institutions; says over 100 schemes were analysed. Every listed scheme and the criteria are already events. No programme statistics.

OECD CRS list, version last updated 20 November 2018: Panama's three visas moved from the high-risk list to a separate table where only Panamanian ID cards with codes PRP-FOR, PRP-SEP and PRP-PA are high-risk; otherwise identical to the October 2018 list. The change is an event. No programme statistics.
OECD CRS list as archived on 21 September 2019: St Kitts and Nevis 'Residence by Investment' no longer listed; otherwise as in November 2018. The change is an event. No programme statistics.
OECD CRS list as archived on 26 June 2020: Malaysia My Second Home no longer listed. The change is an event. No programme statistics.
OECD CRS list as archived in January 2021: Qatar's residence visa for real-estate owners no longer listed. The change is an event. No programme statistics.
OECD CRS list as archived on 20 May 2023: same schemes and text as the January 2021 version (only a typo corrected in the introduction), so no new event. No programme statistics.
